segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: What was the word for what?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: ¿Qué?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: ¿Qué? And do you remember how was to pass?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Is it pasar?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Pasar. And this can also mean like to happen, to pass in the sense of to occur. How do you say he passes?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Pasa.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. And she passes?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Pasa.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: And it passes?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Pasa.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. And if you want to say what passes, meaning what happens, what's going on, what is happening?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Ah. I remembered it now. I went through the whole process and I remember people saying ¿qué pasó?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Ah, this is the past! We said that when you emphasize that o on the end, it's actually the version for he, she, it in the past. So ¿qué pasó? is what happened? And we will look at this later. But what, what's happening? What is happening?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: ¿Qué pasa?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. So if you want to say I want to know what's going on, I want to know what's happening, I want to know what's passing?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Quiero saber qué pasa.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Quiero saber qué pasa. I want to know what's happening. Good.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: There's one more thing we need to know about the present, and it's going to fill in happily a gray area for us, which you might be wondering already. How did we get tiene—he, she, it, you formal has or have—and then the other versions, tienen, tienes, from tener?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: To want is querer. What is I want?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Quiero.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Quiero. So how does querer become quiero?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So there's something else we need to know about the present to understand this, and then we can manage the present completely. So what's happening is that when we have an e in the to form of the verb, like in tener, to have, like in querer, to want, when we have an e inside of the verb that's part of the root, not part of the ending, not that -er, that doesn't count, but the e in ten- and the e in quer- of querer.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: When we stress it, when we emphasize it, it often splits. Most of the time it splits into an ie under the stress of that accent.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Under the stress when we say querer, we have the accent on the end, we have the accent on the ending. Then when we take off that -er and we put -o, we would have quero, but when we stress down on that e, it splits and it becomes quiero.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: The same for tener. We would have tene for he has, but when we stress down on that e, it splits and it becomes tiene.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: The same for come. We have venir. But when we say he comes, she comes, it comes, you formal come, it would be vene, but it becomes viene.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Now it's not happening with tengo, vengo because we can say the n and the g kind of holds it up. So this is probably why it got saved. But otherwise it splits.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Now, this might seem kind of an abstract thing to get your head around, but what is very helpful is that we have this between words in English and Spanish. We can identify this between words in English and Spanish. For example,

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: we have a word that we use for time in English, but only in music. Do you know what is this word?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: A word we use for time, but only in music. When you speak about the time, the rhythm of music, you talk about its...

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Beat.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Not beat, but tempo.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Now, time in Spanish is tiempo. You see the difference between tempo and tiempo, other than the Spanish pronunciation, is that the e has split into ie.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So you can even see it between words in English and Spanish. Concert in Spanish... concert in Spanish is... try to do the same thing.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Concierto.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Concierto. Good. You stuck an -o to make it sound more Spanish and you split that e: concierto. November is noviembre. So this will help us remember.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So this happens most of the time. We already saw places that it doesn't happen. We saw very briefly the verb llegar, which was to arrive, and we said llego, I arrive. We saw esperar, which was to wait or to hope: espero. There it's not happening.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: But most of the time it's going to happen. We saw it happening with tener, which became tiene (he, she, it, you formal), tienen (they or you plural), tienes (you informal). We saw it happening with venir, to come: viene, vienes, vienen.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Another verb that we see this with is pensar. What do you think pensar means?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Thoughtful.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: But it's a verb. There's no verb to thoughtful, is there?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Ah. Well, to think.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Yes. That's it, to think. It's very useful for us to group words into families. So verb is a family.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So when you decide what type of word it is, then you narrow down the possible behaviors of that word, and you manage to manage it much easier. And making that very clearly, that connection, is really, really helpful for you. To think, pensar.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So if you say I think, how is it going to be?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Pienso.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. It would be penso, but you stress down on that e and it splits into ie and you get pienso, pienso. How is he thinks, or she thinks, or it thinks, or you formal?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Piense.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: This sounds like vowel harmony. I mean, it sounds nice, piense, because we have ie and then we want to put an e next to it because it matches, but that's Turkish grammar. You must know where you are with any verb, and to know where you are you must go back to the to form, then you are confident.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: So was pensar, not pensar, not penser.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: No, pensar. So you must go back then, then you feel confident. Otherwise, the base is going to affect what vowel you want to put on.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Piensa.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Piensa. You informal?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Piensas.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. What do you think?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: ¿Qué piensas?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Yeah. ¿Qué piensas? This is useful verb as well, actually, because if you say I think to eat, it means I plan on eating. You can say I think to eat, that simple. I think to eat, how would it sound?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Pienso comer.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Pienso comer. I think to eat later is I plan on eating later. So how would you say I plan on eating later?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Pienso comer tarde.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: That means I, I plan on eating late, which is fine, but later is more late. And more is related to massive.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Más tarde.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Pienso comer más tarde. I plan on eating later. So you can use it like that as well.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: We saw venir also splits, with the exception of vengo. He comes, she comes, you formal, how would that be?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Viene.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Viene. They?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Vienen.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Vienen. You informal?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Vienes.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Do you remember how was when?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Cuándo.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Cuándo. When are you coming?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: ¿Cuándo vienes?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: ¿Cuándo vienes?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Entender, entender means to understand. You can use comprender if you forget it, but entender is better. It's more common.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: But comprender is easier because it's sounds like comprehend, and also in comprender the e doesn't split. I, I understand is comprendo. But with entender, it does split.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So you can use comprender, but most common in Spanish is entender for understand, and here the e does split. So how would you say I understand?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Entiendo.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Entiendo. Entiendo. How would you say he understands?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Entiende.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Entiende. Good. They?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Entienden.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Entienden.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Perder, perder means to lose. It's kind of related to perish. There is a connection there, or perishable food, you know, food that is that rots, you know, real food. Perder, to lose. I lose?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Pierdo.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Pierdo. Good. The process is perder, perdo, maybe it splits, pierdo. Good. I lose it?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Lo pierdo.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Lo pierdo. Good. I lose them?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Los pierdo.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Los pierdo. Good.
